title: What this book is
text: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.
body: God-breathed is a strange, physical word, and Paul chose it. Scripture is not a transcript dictated to secretaries, and it is not a collection of religious opinion; it is human writing that God breathed out through.
Notice what it is for. Four uses, and two of them — reproof and correction — assume the book will tell you that you are wrong. A Bible only ever used for comfort is being used at half strength.
The aim at the end is not information but equipment. You do not finish a passage having learned something; you finish it having been fitted for something.
question: When did Scripture last correct you, rather than confirm you?
practice: Read a chapter this week asking one question only: what does this ask of me?
prayer: God, you breathed this out. Teach me, and correct me where I need it.

title: One story, two halves
text: Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
body: On the road to Emmaus, Jesus gives the definitive lesson in how to read the Old Testament, and Luke does not record a word of it. What he records is the method: all of it, about him.

That is the key that turns the Old Testament from a strange anthology into the first two thirds of one story. The sacrifices, the temple, the exile, the kings who all fall short — they are not detours before the good part.
It also stops you plundering the Old Testament for slogans. A promise made to Israel in exile is not a promise about your visa, and reading it as one skips over what it actually says about God.
question: Which half of the Bible do you avoid, and what has that cost you?
practice: Read Isaiah 53 and then Mark 15, in that order, in one sitting.
prayer: Jesus, open the Scriptures to me the way you opened them on that road.

title: Reading in context
text: They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading.
body: Gave the sense. A crowd who had lost the language needed more than the words — they needed what the words meant, in order, in context.
Three questions do most of the work: who is this written to, what has just happened, and what comes immediately after. A verse lifted out of that is a quotation, not a text.
This is the difference between a verse that comforts you and a passage that changes you. The first can be printed on a mug. The second has to be read with its neighbours.
question: What is your favourite verse actually about, in its own chapter?
practice: Take a verse you love. Read the whole chapter around it and write one sentence on what it is really saying.
prayer: Lord, I have used your words to say my own things. Give me the sense of them.

title: Read to obey
text: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
body: James's word for the self-deception of the hearer is strong: it means to reason yourself around something. Hearing a great deal of teaching can leave a person feeling obedient.
The test he gives next is a mirror — you look, you see, you walk away and forget what you look like. Bible reading that produces no action is not neutral; it is a habit of forgetting yourself.
So the discipline is small and boring: one thing per passage, done this week, checked.
question: What was the last thing Scripture told you to do that you actually did?
practice: End every reading this week with a single sentence beginning "So today I will…"
prayer: God, keep me from being a person who agrees with you and does nothing.

title: Keeping at it
text: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
body: A lamp for the feet lights the next step, not the whole road. That is a modest, honest picture of what Scripture does — and it is the reason daily reading beats occasional reading.
Psalm 119 is 176 verses about loving a book, written by someone under pressure. Its endurance is not enthusiasm; it is the repeated, unspectacular return.
Pick a plan you can finish rather than one that impresses you. A gospel in three weeks, read, beats a year plan abandoned in February.
question: What would a Bible habit look like that you could still be doing in a year?
practice: Start one reading plan in the Bible tab today. Choose the shortest one.
prayer: Lord, light the next step. I will keep coming back for the one after it.
